'First to use autoregressive diffusion models for DAG generation' is too broad given prior AR-diffusion hybrid models (ARDMs, EDGE, GRAPHARM)
Surrogate-based evaluation is indirect but paper does not acknowledge this as a limitation or calibrate the evaluation chain
Conclusion is one paragraph with no discussion of limitations, bounded claims, or future directions
Permutation invariance argument does not explicitly connect set-based intra-layer processing to the invariance claim
Layer partition definition V(l+1) is ambiguous between 'any predecessor' and 'all predecessors' in V(<=l)
Conditional independence assumption in the P(G) factorization is not discussed despite being a strong modeling choice
Adaptive edge prior sensitivity to inaccurate layer-size predictions is not analyzed
paper_b_weakness_points: 'State-of-the-art across all datasets' and 'first Transformer with linear complexity in both L and M' are unbounded to evaluated baselines and lack external verification
All 32 tasks report single-seed point estimates despite seed variation shown in appendix making small-margin improvements unverifiable
Swin4TS uses L=512 while several baselines were designed for L=96; asymmetric input-length advantage is not fully controlled or transparently reported
Ablation gains of 2-3% MSE are within observed seed-variation range; only two datasets used for ablation; no significance testing
Claim that time-series and image patches share structural similarity is asserted with weak arguments; fundamental differences (causality, trend/seasonality) are not addressed
Conclusion claims time series and images 'can be modeled using the same framework' without any limitations; TNT4TS evidence on only 4 ETT datasets is too thin to support the broad claim
Variable z_i reused ambiguously across equations; hierarchical output shape mapping and padding strategy for non-power-of-2 inputs not explained

paper_a_strength_points: Novel and practically motivated problem definition (SLNC) that formally relaxes standard SSNC requirements for label quantity and per-class selection
Consistent 10–20% absolute accuracy gains over all baselines across 7 benchmark datasets under extreme label sparsity (1–4 labels/class)
Practical computational efficiency: LP-ELI and SGC-ELI complete in under 3 seconds versus CGPN's >48 seconds or timeout
Honest acknowledgment of the key limitation that ELI requires knowing the number of classes c in advance
paper_b_strength_points: Novel shape abstraction reduces vocabulary from 7371 typed subgraphs to 347 shapes, directly addressing the vocabulary-size bottleneck of motif-based methods
Strong quantitative evidence that MAGNet recovers uncommon shapes and matches training shape distribution far better than baselines (Figure 1)
Best AAO model on GuacaMol benchmarks (FCD 0.76, KL 0.95) while operating from shape-level abstractions
Superior coverage of atom/bond allocation space for shapes versus baselines, confirmed by MMD quantification (Figure 2)

Principled multi-Laplacian regularization framework with mathematical grounding in graph signal denoising theory
Comprehensive evaluation across 7 benchmark datasets with 10 runs and ablation studies isolating each component
10-20% absolute accuracy improvement over baselines in the ultra-sparse (1-2 labels per class) regime

Thorough multi-dimensional evaluation covering structural diversity, standard benchmarks, allocation quality, and cross-dataset transfer
Useful diagnostic analysis showing FCD is insensitive to structural diversity (104-molecule subset achieves FCD=0.89, higher than most generative models)
Ablation studies cleanly quantifying contribution of normalizing flow (+0.11 FCD) and typed connectivity (+0.10 FCD)
Zero-shot cross-dataset transfer to QM9, GuacaMol, ChEMBL, and L1000 with up to 20% improvement over baselines
Reproducibility commitment: code, detailed hyperparameters, and standard public benchmarks provided

paper_a_weakness_points: Zero variance (0.00 std) in LP-ELI/SGC-ELI results at the #1 label setting is unexplained and undermines experimental credibility
Incomplete baseline comparisons: domain-shift/robustness methods omitted despite their relevance to sparse random labels
Requires known number of classes c in advance, contradicting real-world motivation; no sensitivity experiments for mis-specified c
KNN graph construction for A_{GH} underspecified in main text, fully described only in appendix
Related work reads as a chronological list rather than a structured taxonomy organized by comparison axes
Contribution C3 ('we show 10-20% improvement') is a purely empirical result, not a conceptual contribution
Typos and grammatical errors throughout (e.g., 'trade of blow', 'four steps' listed where five items follow)
No statistical significance tests for the claimed 10-20% improvement despite high baseline variance
paper_b_weakness_points: "First to freely featurise shapes" claim in C3 is an unsupported chronological priority assertion without prior-art verification
Train-test distribution mismatch from two-stage VAE+flow training is unanalyzed and not disclosed as a limitation
Benchmark overclaim: "outperforms all other graph-based baselines" is contradicted by the paper's own Table 1 (MoLeR scores higher on FCD and KL)
Ablation studies only evaluate benchmark metrics, not the core structural diversity claim, leaving causal evidence for diversity gains missing
Conclusion (7 lines) contains no explicit limitations, omitting known issues such as lower FCD than MoLeR and 75% QM9 coverage gap
Notation ambiguity: S overloaded to denote both the shape multiset and an individual shape's binary adjacency matrix
Encoder/decoder architecture details missing (transformer heads, dropout, activation), reducing reproducibility
Minor typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'asseses', 'those model')
